body: License plates are white with blue letters, though the blue can be hard to see. Government plates are green.
Cambodia has two Google cars: one with a short, triple-ridged antenna and one white-striped car with yellow and white side stripes, unique to Cambodia.
Cambodia drives on the right side, while Thailand is on the left and Laos also drives right.
The official language is Khmer, with its own curvy, intricate script distinct from Thai or Lao.
Common poles include concrete ladder-style or round concrete ones with holes. Thailand uses square poles, unlike Cambodia.
Typical bollards are stone with red-white stripes or red tops and reflectors; designs vary regionally.
Road markers are stone with a white base and rounded red top, showing road numbers and town distances.
Chevrons are black with yellow arrows, unlike other Southeast Asian countries that use yellow with black.
Cambodian roads have yellow center lines and occasional white outer lines, similar to Thailand.
Many Cambodian roads are unpaved; only major and urban routes are typically surfaced.
Traditional houses are wooden on stilts, often with vertical planks and multiple layered roofs.
Typical stilt houses have red-brown, blue, or ochre walls with bright blue details, though newer homes vary.
Roofs are often orange or red tile with ornate edges, though metal roofs and modern materials are common too.
Cambodia is mostly Buddhist, with temples featuring ornate roofs and frequent Buddhist flags.
Beer ads for Angkor, Anchor, and Cambodia Beer are widely seen across the country.
CPP signs are bright blue and often feature three prominent party leaders’ portraits.
Older Google coverage uses the low-quality 'Shitcam', recognizable by its brown tint and circular blur.
Street View is mainly found around Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, and Battambang areas.
The Shitcam coverage only exists in the southwestern half of Cambodia.
The central plain is flat, agricultural, and dotted with villages and farms.
The northeast has more natural vegetation, fewer farms, and hilly terrain.
The southwest is Cambodia’s most elevated area, with hills, forests, and coastal villages.
White sandy soil is common southeast of Phnom Penh; it can vary from bright white to beige.
Near Thailand’s border, a northern ridgeline with red soil and flat foregrounds is visible.
Rubber plantations appear near Phnom Penh, Ban Lung, and Pech Sreada, with neat uniform tree rows.
Only Road 48 has black-and-white bollards; these resemble Thai ones, so use other clues too.
The Kiri Sakor road is half-paved, with one paved side and red unpaved soil on the other.
Southwestern jungle roads are unpaved, red-soiled, and surrounded by dense vegetation and hills.
The Phnum Samkos area is mountainous, lush, and often overcast, with unpaved brown roads.
Triangular red-striped bollards appear only in the southwest, especially along Road 4 and national parks.
Road 4 is known for wide, reddish-brown shoulders that darken near the coast.
Oil palm plantations occur only near Preah Nob along Road 4 and nearby rural roads.
Preah Monivong National Park features white rocky soil, dark green bushes, and a highland plateau landscape.
Road 41 southwest of Phnom Penh runs NNE, with a wide gravel surface and visible distant hills.
Unique power poles with triple beams and single-side insulators appear on Road 6 and 5 near Sisophon.
West of Sisophon, power poles have insulators on both sides but keep the same design as before.
The southern Road 76 features dark asphalt, clear lines, and hilly jungle terrain under cloudy skies.
The northern Road 76 is wide and unpaved, passing through semi-open forest with skies clearing northward.
The Pech Sreada region has orange soil and dry-season rubber plantations creating a unique appearance.
Angkor Wat near Siem Reap is a vast stone temple complex with dark, historic architecture.
